components.html:
The purpose:
It is our goal to help you learn and understand stitch patterning on YOUR machine.
There are many makes and models of knitting machines in use. It would be impossible to create courses and exercises for each machine.
Although the names and position of the buttons and levers vary from machine to machine, the functionality of these machines is very much the same.
It is important for you to identify, learn and master each of the available techniques for YOUR machine. Armed with that knowledge, you can add stitch patterning to your machine knitting toolbox to create the knitwear of your dreams.
The format:
  1. Using your machine manual, explore and discover all of the buttons and levers on your machine. Record the names and location of each item as related to automatic stitch patterning
    • The Automatic Needle Selection Device
    • Cam/Carriage Levers and buttons
  2. Practice each of the most common stitch patterns
    • Use the suggested stitch patterns or patterns provided with your machine
    • Put each of the previously identified buttons/levers to work and record YOUR settings for each technique
Terminology:
Being US based, the terms we use may differ from those you know. (we spell color without a U) We will provide photos and video as much as possible to help with any language barrier. One term that we tend to use interchangeably is Cam/Carriage.
Abbreviations:
Although common in vintage machine knitting manuals, patterns, and documents, we do not use abbreviations. Check the Knit it Now Glossary for any "mystery" abbreviations you may encounter on your journey to master your machine.
We encourage you to work through all the exercises .. don't just watch videos. Study YOUR manual step by step. Answer the questions presented here in this course. Sit down at your machine and try the exercises. The best way to learn something new (and have it stick in your mind) is to DO IT!
As you are probably aware, the Brand names of machines have changed over the years. We will use the terms Brother, Silver/Singer throughout this course. Substitute the name of your machine where appropriate.

One of the many advantages of machine knitting is the ability to quickly and easily knit in pattern. Textured stitch patterns, multi-color patterns can all be quickly produced with the help of automatic patterning devices. Using Punchcard or electronics, the machine automatically selects needles for pattern knitting.
FACT: To create stitch patterns on any machine, it is a combination of the position of the needles PLUS the carriage settings.
In order to work in pattern on any machine (manual or automatic) you must remember (AND UNDERSTAND) this fact.
It doesn't matter if the needles are being positioned by hand or by a patterning device, the correct setting on the carriage (cam) will produce stitch patterns.

Your Challenge:

  • Locate and identify the levers and buttons on your machine (use your manual)
  • Learn about needle positions and their impact on knitting in pattern
  • Learn the differences between the various stitch techniques
  • Apply the settings for YOUR machine to produce the stitch techniques
  • Fill-in-the-blanks as you work through the investigative part of this course. Your answers will be remembered and used in the practice part of the course. This will help you apply YOUR specific notes and customize the practices
Do this before getting started:
  • Have your manual handy (get a free copy here)
  • Make sure your machine is in good working order
    • Clean and oiled (see your manual)
    • is in good shape. (A flat sponge bar will cause any number of problems, especially when knitting in pattern)
  • Have available lots of yarn appropriate for your machine. Choose smooth, light color yarn

As you work through the sections of this course you will be prompted with fill-in-the-blanks questions.
Provided are the most common names and descriptions for various machines, but you are encouraged to use your manual to find the answer.
Enter in the answer that will make sense to you when you use your Cheat Sheet.
After completing the material in the course, you'll be able to print out your personal Cheat Sheet for future reference.
Let's get started:

components.html:
These devices tell the knitting carriage (cam) to knit stitches or not knit stitches on the needles in different knitting positions.
No matter how the needles get into specific positions (with punchcard, electronics or by hand), these devices will control how the stitches are formed.
Imagine the underside of your knitting carriage.
There are tracks that the butt of the needles follow.
The Cam levers/buttons open and close gates that allow the needle butts to travel through specific channels.
It's the movement of the needles thru these channels that either knit the stitch, tuck the stitch (yarn over the needle), slip the stitch (yarn under the needle), transfer the stitch(lace) or knit in a second color (fairisle)

The is the heart of the magic of patterning with a knitting machine.

TRY THIS
  1. Remove your carriage and engage the Cam buttons/levers.
  2. Turn the carriage over
  3. Observe what happens underneath and imagine the movement of the needles through the tracks.

Why care about needle positions?
With automatic patterning, your machine (as instructed by the patterning device) will automatically select needles. The black/white, hole/no hole, on/off settings of the patterning device, positions the needles for stitch patterning.
But is is important that you understand needle positions on your machine. You may want to set up manual patterning for a few rows. With Brother/Knit King Machines, you may need to re-position needles after ripping rows.
Take time to understand the positions and the terminology of the positions.
Depending on your machine there are 4 or more needle positions. There are letters engraved on the needlebed indicating the various positions. These letters can differ between machines, but more importantly you must recognize what they represent.
Throughout this course we will try to refer to the function of each position, rather than the letter. In vintage machine knitting documentation, abbreviations are often used for these settings. We will not use these in this course.

Although the terms, buttons, dials and levers differ between the various brands of machines, the results are the same. We can knit beautiful, colorful and textured fabrics "automatically".
The Patterning device takes "input" from a punchcard, or electronically and "translates" on/off, 0/1, hole/no hole to an action that will position needles on the needlebed to create stitch patterns.
However, the basic knitting logic of creating stitch patterns is approached somewhat differently by Brother/Knit King and Singer/Silver/Studio machines.
Once the stitch pattern is set up and the carriages are set correctly, the actual knitting differs slightly.
It is important that you to understand YOUR machine.
Once you are familiar with your machine this difference is only obvious and impact-ful if you have multiple machines from different brands. THE DIFFERENCE:
  • Brother machines pre-select needles for the following row. You can see the position of the needles.
  • Silver/Singer machines memorize the pattern internally and the needles move into their assigned positions the pass of the carriage. (no previewing)

Brother/Knit King Brother machines pre-select the needles in the positions that are dictated by the patterning device.
  • On the initial, set up row, the needles are selected, but the stitches are knit plain and are not formed in the stitch pattern.
  • On the next pass of the carriage, the stitches will be formed according to the pattern and carriage settings.
  • Subsequent rows will form the stitches according to pattern AND pre-select the needles for the next row.
Singer/Silver/Studio These machines have a memory wheel on the carriage, that memorizes the stitch pattern for the next row.
  • On the first pass of the carriage (the setup row), the knitting is plain and the memory wheel records the pattern.
  • On the next pass of the carriage, the stitches are formed in pattern AND the memory wheel prepares for the following row.

There is an arrangement of the needle selection mechanism, and the cam levers and buttons that is specific to knitting plain knitting on your machine.
You've probably already discovered this setting, but if you are new, let's identify YOUR settings.
Many a new knitter gets frustrated when a button or lever is changed in error and they have a problem knitting in plain stockinette.
This will become second nature to you, but while you are still learning, take time EVERY TIME to double check your settings.
Keep a cheat sheet near your machine and double check before knitting.

  • Hold position: {Position_hold}
The HOLD setting has many uses in machine knitting.
From Free Pass to Short Row shaping , using HOLD is an essential skill.

TRY THIS (Single hold button)
  1. With no yarn in your carriage, set the carriage for plain knitting
  2. Pull a few needles to "{Position_hold}" (hold) position
  3. Set your carriage to hold in both directions
  4. Pass the carriage left and right
The needles should remain in hold position.
TRY THIS (Left/Right hold button)
  1. With no yarn in your carriage, set the carriage for plain knitting
  2. Carriage on the right
  3. Pull a few needles to "{Position_hold}" (hold) position
  4. Set the carriage to HOLD LEFT
  5. Pass the carriage left
    The needles should remain in hold position
  6. Pass the carriage right
    The needles should return to working position
  7. Repeat, alternating left and right until you are comfortable with the settings

Try this with yarn
  1. Cast on and knit for a few rows
  2. Carriage on the right
  3. Pull a few needles to "{Position_hold}" (hold) position
  4. Set the carriage to HOLD
  5. Pass the carriage left
    The held needles should remain in hold position
  6. Notice that the working yarn travels OVER the needles in hold

Tuck Practice 1
  1. Choose an stitch pattern for tuck (mostly black, no 2 white squares next to each other)
  2. Using a lightweight, light color yarn, cast on 40-60 stitches with any method
  3. Hang weights
  4. Knit a few rows, ending with the carriage on the LEFT.
  5. Be sure to bring your carriage far enough out, so the pattern is "read"
  6. Insert your punchcard or start your electronic stitch pattern
  7. Set your {selection_mechanism} selection mechanism
  8. With the pattern "locked" on the first row, knit 1 row LEFT to RIGHT
  9. Using your {cam_lever_tuck} set the carriage to tuck in both directions
  10. Begin to pattern by moving the carriage to the LEFT.
  11. Continue to knit in pattern for 20-40 rows
  12. Cancel the {cam_lever_tuck} tuck setting
  13. Cancel the {selection_mechanism} selection mechanism
  14. Knit a few rows plain and bind off
Notes:
  • Tuck requires weight
  • Be sure to take the carriage past the point where the automatic patterning device can "read/memorize" the pattern (see your manual)
  • For success, knit at a slower pace than plain knitting
  • Maintain an even rhythm

WEAVING is a technique that places decorative strands across a base of knitting (usually stockinette). Built-in weaving brushes keep the weaving yarn in place and prevents it from floating up and jamming the carriage while knitting in pattern.
Automatic patterning machines will select needles and put them in position for the weaving yarn to "lay-in" across the needles. The weaving yarn does not form stitches, but is secured by the knitting in decorative sequences.
Weaving is a great way to use novelty yarns or yarn that may be too thick for your machine.

Don't Skip This Video

No Brushes?

You can work Knit Weave on manual machines and machines with no brushes

Knit WeavePractice 1
  1. Choose a stitch pattern for KNIT WEAVE
  2. Using a lightweight, light color yarn, cast on 40-60 stitches with any method
  3. Hang weights
  4. Knit a few rows, ending with the carriage on the LEFT.
  5. Be sure to bring your carriage far enough out, so the pattern is "read"
  6. Insert your punchcard or start your electronic stitch pattern
  7. Set your {selection_mechanism} selection mechanism
  8. With the pattern "locked" on the first row, knit 1 row LEFT to RIGHT(to memorize/record the pattern)
  9. Engage your Weaving Brushes
  10. Position the weaving yarn on the LEFT as shown in your manual * (the weaving yarn will be on the side of the carriage in the direction of knitting)
  11. Begin to pattern by moving the carriage to the LEFT.
  12. Switch the weaving yarn to the opposite side (RIGHT)
  13. Knit to the RIGHT
  14. Continue to knit in pattern, alternating the weaving yarn left and right for 20-40 rows
  15. Cancel the {selection_mechanism} selection mechanism
  16. Knit a few rows plain and bind off
Notes:
  • * Most manuals advise you to thread the weaving yarn thru the tension mast. Many machine knitters place their weaving yarn on the floor at their feet and manually tension the yarn
  • Notice that you are not using any Cam/Carriage settings, you have just engaged your {selection_mechanism} Selection mechanism to select needles.

Depending on your machine, this is a setting (or stop) on the cam lever on the carriage to enable you to knit lace-like patterns with a very thin yarn or thread. THREAD (PUNCH) LACE creates a lace appearance without transferring stitches to make holes. It also knits with NO FLOATS.

How does it work?
In the solid sections of the design, both yarns knit together.
In the "lace" sections, only the fine yarn knits forming the appearance of holes

Some standard gauge (4.5mm) machines have an optional carriage that automatically transfers stitches to create eyelet holes.
NOTE: Only Standard Gauge machines have lace carriages

Because of the way the stitch patterns are formed, stitch patterns (punchcard or electronic) for lace carriages differ from other stitch patterns (tuck, slip, fairisle).
The patterning device selects and positions the needles. Combined with the correct carriage settings PLUS the lace carriage "automatic" lace is magical.

Different models have different approaches to lace carriages:


Brother Lace Carriage Brother lace carriage is used alternately with the main knitting carriage. Based on instruction from the patterning device (electronic or punchcard), the lace carriage selects and transfers stitches. The main carriage is then used to knit the row
Singer/Silver Lace Carriage Silver/Singer lace carriages work independently of the main knitting carriage. The lace carriage, selects, transfers and knits the row.

components.html:
The Garter Carriage is a Brother/KnitKing Standard Gauge Accessory. This fabulous motorized knitting carriage allows you to incorporate purl stitches on the flat bed knitting machine without using a ribber.
There were different models of G-Carriages manufactured for specific machines. If you are unsure do some research to confirm your G-carriage is compatible with your knitting machine. Both punch card and electronic machines were offered G-carriages as optional accessories.

As with any other stitch patterns, forming knit an purl stitches on the same row is controlled by the Patterning Device, and the Carriage buttons.
